findings.claim: "Fourth Lateran Council defines transubstantiation" overstates; Lateran IV used the word in its creed, and the dogmatic definition with canons is Trent (1551), which is also absent from the history.
findings.evidence: Lateran IV canon 1 (Firmiter, 1215): 'transubstantiatis pane in corpus, et vino in sanguinem'. Trent Sess. XIII (11 October 1551) ch. 4 and canon 2 define transubstantiation; CCC 1376 quotes Trent, not Lateran IV, as the definition.
findings.fix: "1215: Fourth Lateran Council adopts the word 'transubstantiation' in its creed." and add {"when":"1551","what":"Council of Trent defines the Real Presence and transubstantiation against the Reformers."}

findings.claim: 'Fourth Lateran Council defines transubstantiation' overstates it. Lateran IV used the word in its creed; the dogmatic definition came at Trent. The line also makes a specifically Roman doctrine the sacramental pole's milestone, though the Lutherans and Orthodox placed at that pole reject transubstantiation.
findings.evidence: Lateran IV, canon 1 Firmiter (1215): 'transubstantiatis pane in corpus et vino in sanguinem'. Trent, Session XIII (11 Oct 1551), ch. 4 and canon 2, defines the doctrine (Denzinger 802; 1642, 1652). McGrath, Christian Theology, on the term's history.
findings.fix: {when: '1215', what: 'Fourth Lateran Council writes "transubstantiated" into its creed; Trent (1551) will define the doctrine.'}

findings.claim: 'Fourth Lateran Council defines transubstantiation' overstates it; the Catholic apologist will correct you.
findings.evidence: Lateran IV (1215) uses 'transubstantiatis' in its opening creed; the dogmatic definition with canons is Trent, Session XIII (1551).
findings.fix: 'Fourth Lateran Council uses the word transubstantiation in its creed; Trent defines it in 1551.'
